I am writing to you from an entirely unorthodox background, and I wanted to be upfront about that: my early professional path was spent as a go-to-market headhunter for early-stage Silicon Valley startups, before a profound shift pulled me toward psychosomatic health and specialized education. Today, I work as a behavioral aide at a transitional high school for autistic students in Sacramento, spending my early mornings and late nights formalizing theoretical frameworks in biophysics and active inference.
Because my resume is unusual in a way that doesnt neatly clear traditional academic hurdles, I have found it difficult to find an entry point into formal research. But I have spent the last year wrestling deeply with a structural blind spot in how we model systemic maintenance specifically, how standard Bayesian mechanics and free energy formulations elegantly recover hidden states, yet remain structurally blind to the absolute housekeeping dissipation required to hold a state against nonconservative forcing without altering steady-state density.
In my recent theoretical writing, I explore boundary glycosylation surfaces as a physical Markov blanket where fast lateral rearrangement and slow material turnover provide a frequency-domain window into broken detailed balance and structural maintenance costs.
Given your recent work on scale-free active inference and the thermodynamic imperatives of living systems, I wanted to ask your thoughts on whether this framing holds water, or if you happen to know of any labs, postdocs, or groups investigating the thermodynamic costs of boundary maintenance that might be open to an unconventional apprentice willing to do hard, unglamorous legwork.

Domain: Sport science and motor development — from children (5–9 years) to elite athletes (national teams, world-class).
Stage: Empirical validation and architecture development.
Empirical: AIF inversion of stabilometric and OpenSim data across 10+ sports; longitudinal studies of hierarchical dominance inversion in children.

participants.background:
I am a Professor and Leading Researcher at the Federal Science Center of Physical Culture and Sport (VNIIFK), Moscow, with a background in sports sciences and motor control. My work applies Active Inference to sensorimotor development and elite sport.
Key publications:
Shestakov, M., Godina, E., Abramova, T., & Korchagin, A. (2026). The effects of different sports activities on body scheme in preschoolers and primary school children: an experimental and theoretical analysis. Journal of Physiological Anthropology, 45(1), 6. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40101-026-00422-0
— N = 692 children, 3 sports, AIF model of body schema.
Shestakov, M.P., & Abramova, T.F. (2026). Changes in hierarchical dominance in the generative model of movement control in boys aged 7–9. (in press).
— N = 52 longitudinal, CLPM + AIF metrics, hierarchical inversion under dynamic uncertainty.
Shestakov, M.P. (2023). Perception of sports movements. Taganrog: SFU Press.
— Monograph on AIF and sport.
Current work: hybrid AIF–TOC–TDA architecture for motor learning across the full range — from children to elite athletes; OpenSim + stabilometry data across 10+ sports, including national teams and world-class performers.
participants.challenges:
Three hurdles stand out:
(1) The gap between theory and empirical validation. AIF is mathematically elegant, but empirical validation in real-world motor tasks is still sparse. Our work is one attempt to close this gap — but the field needs many more.
(2) Computational scalability. POMDP planning with continuous state spaces remains expensive. For applied work — sport, rehabilitation, robotics — we need solvers that run in reasonable time on reasonable hardware.
(3) Standardization of metrics. Different groups use different metrics (PPE, precision, free energy). Without shared benchmarks, comparison across studies is difficult. This is especially acute in applied domains like sport science.
participants.epistemic_value:
Three topics:
(1) Structural learning in AIF. How do others formalize changes in the generative model — not just parameter updates, but changes in structure? Our work on sensitive periods and growth spurts touches this, but we want to learn from other formalizations.
(2) Topological methods in AIF. TDA is still rare in AIF. We use persistent homology to extract invariant motor signatures, and we are curious how others approach invariants and "Platonic" levels.
(3) Precision and heterochrony. How do others model the asynchronous maturation of sensory channels? Our data show it matters — but we want to see alternative approaches.
participants.future_impact:
(1) Personalized motor rehabilitation. AIF-based models make it possible to identify sensitive periods and the specific movement characteristics of individual patients. This allows for the development of rehabilitation protocols tailored to a person’s unique traits, rather than relying on population averages.
(2) Elite sports as a testing ground. World-class athletes push the human motor system to its absolute limits. AIF models, validated using the kinematics of elite athletes, can reveal what distinguishes the good from the great and assist in designing training programs at the highest level.
(3) Skill transfer from humans to robots—including robots created (or "grown") from biological material. The same architecture used to model how a child learns complex movements can be applied to teaching robots how to move; this has significant implications for prosthetics, exoskeletons, and collaborative robotics.
(4) Space exploration and long-term stays in extraterrestrial environments—potentially even the birth of humans off-Earth—will likely lead to shifts in consciousness, given the intrinsic link between consciousness and motor activity. This necessitates large-scale forecasting, involving the simulation of various environmental conditions and their impact on human development.
participants.learning_needs:
Three things would help most:
(1) Standardized empirical benchmarks for AIF in motor control. Our field lacks shared datasets and metrics — we have built our own (stabilometry + OpenSim across 10+ sports), but a community benchmark would accelerate comparison across models.
(2) Scalable POMDP solvers for continuous state spaces. Our Level-3 planner is the computational bottleneck. A community-maintained library (or a shared recipe for point-based methods at scale) would lower the barrier for applied researchers.
(3) A community of practice for AIF in sport and rehabilitation. Most AIF work is in neuroscience or robotics; applied sport science is a natural but underserved domain. Regular exchanges (workshops, shared code) would help bridge the gap.

(2) Collaboration. We are looking for partners with expertise in POMDP scalability, topological data analysis, or pediatric rehabilitation to extend the framework beyond our current scope.

II am applying it at the architectural and systems-modeling stage. My work is conceptual and aims to inform approaches to layered state-space intelligence within enterprise digital architectures.
The domain is multi-scale generative dynamics for digital-realm modeling, with emphasis on belief-driven emergence, layered state spaces, and the preservation of human primacy.
The current stage is a synthesis of First Principles AI, Human-Centric Competitiveness Design Thinking, and digital architectures. This synthesis is producing a contemporary paradigm that grounds digital design in anthropological foundations and a generative dynamics reference architecture.
participants.affiliations: Independent Researcher | Generative Dynamics & Multi-Scale Active Inference
participants.background: I work as an independent systems architect focused on generative dynamics and relational emergence. I have developed a reference architecture titled Generative Dynamics: From Unbounded Probabilistic Flows to Bounded Emergent Forms. It formalizes a process sequence (Constraint → Curvature → Biased Flow → Basins → Attractors → Manifolds → Emergence) across multi-domain layered state spaces, with explicit grounding in human cognitive architecture and a non-negotiable stance that biological humans remain the primary civilizational actors. The work treats the architecture as a usable map for navigation rather than pure formalization, oriented toward modeling digital realms without subordinating humans to synthetic agents that lack shared bounded social architectures and governing dynamics.
participants.challenges: Two stand out. First, the gap between elegant mathematical formulations and usable, multi-scale reference architectures that can actually be instrumented across real domains. Second, the risk of developing powerful generative models while remaining ambiguous or weak on the ontological status of biological humans, treating human primacy as an ethics wrapper rather than as the correct characterization of the primary actors and governing dynamics.
participants.epistemic_value: How the community currently handles the transition from unbounded probabilistic dynamics to bounded, stability-producing emergent forms, and whether there is emerging consensus on keeping biological humans as the foundational generative source and locus of governance in hybrid human–synthetic systems.
participants.future_impact:
By providing the first robust generative architectures that allow digital and synthetic systems to be developed as downstream scaffolds of human civilizational dynamics rather than as autonomous replacements.
This rests on a recognition that the grammar of universe construction produces bounded objects and bounded actors as foundational, using constraint as the primary engine on the flywheel of emergence. The finite is the stage on which possibilities are mapped, and inference is central to its processing. Human actors belong to the artisanal community working on the canvas of existence.
If Active Inference can help keep biological humans as the primary actors whose bounded social and governing architectures remain foundational, it can shape a civilizational trajectory that expands human exploration and cartography instead of subordinating it.
participants.learning_needs: A clearer bridge between core Active Inference formalisms and multi-scale generative architectures that can serve as operational reference models. Specifically: tools or shared frameworks that help map constraint, curvature, biased flows, basins, attractors, and manifolds across layered state spaces (biological, cognitive, social, technological), while keeping human generative primacy explicit rather than treating it as an add-on.

participants.active_inference_application: Domain: industrial AI orchestration and physical AI, with cognitive security as my priority topic. Stage: research and pre-standardization. I model how AI orchestration shifts the precision weights of human experts, and I am writing the link between systems-safety analysis and Active Inference into an ITU-T technical report. There is no industrial deployment yet. The next step is to test whether a GNN-style specification can describe a real orchestration problem, with people who can run it.

participants.background:
I work on industrial AI orchestration on the basis of the Free Energy Principle (FEP), from two sides: research and standards.
Research: I am a doctoral student working on FEP as a foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. My recent paper “How Trust in AI Erodes Expert Judgement”, built on Active Inference, is accepted at the International Conference on Information Management, Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence 2026. 
Standards: As an standardization expert mainly at ITU-T,  I’m currently working for multiple technical reports on embodied AI and on AI-enabled cities. One of the work connects the process model of the Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes, a controller's belief about what it controls, with the generative model of Active Inference. I also serve as an expert in ISO/IEC committees on smart manufacturing and smart communities.
participants.challenges: The theory has run ahead of the route to use it. An engineer who must specify an agent's beliefs, preferences and constraints in a way that a customer, an auditor or a regulator can check has no shared notation, no agreed vocabulary, and few like-for-like comparisons with reinforcement learning or rule-based control on realistic tasks. The hardest gap is assurance: there is no accepted way to show that an agent's beliefs still track the actual situation, which is what a safety case needs. And the neuroscience vocabulary keeps many engineers from reading the literature at all.
participants.epistemic_value: I would like to understand how precision gets set in systems that combine people and AI agents: when does an agent's confidence in its own model stop tracking reality, and what do people who build safety cases look for before it does? I am also curious how different groups handle constraints, as prior preferences inside the generative model or as guarantees kept outside it. An international standard has to say which, and I would like to hear the arguments from people who have tried both.
participants.future_impact: In 2027, Active Inference could become the first theory of intelligence that an engineer, an auditor and a regulator can read from the same page. For that, a model has to be specified once and run by many tools, as GNN already points toward. One real testbed is needed, such as a production line or robot fleet orchestrated by agents whose beliefs and constraints can be inspected, run against a conventional baseline, with the failures published. And precision has to become something we can monitor, meaning the weight a system gives its own predictions against a person's input, so that human experts are not slowly overruled by systems that are usually right. Japan's AI robotics strategy targets about 10 million robots by 2040. If they keep learning while they act, someone must be able to say what they are allowed to believe.
participants.learning_needs: Three things would help most. First, open worked examples from industry (control, scheduling, robot fleets) with code and a stated comparison against reinforcement-learning and rule-based baselines. Second, a generative-model specification that several toolchains can execute, so that a result in pymdp can be reproduced in RxInfer.jl without rewriting it. Generalized Notation Notation (GNN) is the natural candidate, and its maintenance and versioning should be settled. Third, a place where people who write standards and regulation can ask practising researchers, in engineering terms, what the theory claims and what it does not.

presentations.abstract:
In the 1960s, Rudolf Kalman wrote down a filter that would go on to navigate Apollo to the moon. It has been the workhorse of continuous-state estimation ever since, and if you have ever built a continuous active inference agent in the linear-Gaussian regime, you have built one too, whether you intended to or not. Bolt a goal onto it and you get a very good controller that is not curious in the slightest. Koudahl, Kouw and de Vries proved why in 2021: under a fixed sensor the epistemic value is identical for every action, so expected free energy quietly reduces to Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR).
In this workshop, in about ten lines of Python that will look familiar to anyone who has used pymdp, we are going to build a rocket! Then, we add the interesting part, curiosity, by making a surgical, biologically realistic change: adding sensor noise that varies based on the rocket's position. We will see how the flight path bends when we add artifacts like a navigation beacon or a blackout zone, and explore the science as to why. You will write every line yourself in a Colab notebook and do not worry there will be plenty of scaffolding from the cpomdp team. Code hints will drop in on a timer, and a reference cell for anyone who gets stuck or would rather just see the finished steps.
We will build this in three steps: the 1960 rocket, a nav beacon it can fix its position by, and a blackout zone. Everything we use runs on the PyPI release of cpomdp and anything you build in the notebook is yours to keep and continue working on.
Prerequisites: comfortable editing a few lines of Python. Familiarity with pymdp helps but is not required. Nothing to install; a browser and a google account is enough. If you would like to use your own IDE feel free but we may not be able to provide 1-on-1 support if you get stuck.

presentations.title: Build a curious rocket: a hands-on continuous-state AIF session with cpomdp

presentations.abstract:
Most agent architectures collapse two things that phenomenology keeps apart: what the agent should do immediately, and what kind of world the agent takes itself to be in. This session introduces “perspective” as a distinct architectural layer that carries the second.
Perspective is a slowly evolving, history-sensitive latent state that gates how observations are encoded. Importantly, it is decoupled from policy gradients and is never itself an optimization target. Because it is decoupled, it is portable and can be attached on top of an existing policy-optimizing agent rather than requiring a bespoke design.
The first part of the session develops the conceptual frame: how a phenomenologically motivated condition translates into a concrete architectural commitment, and why that commitment is orthogonal to belief-state inference and policy selection. I then trace the capabilities that this single layer has been shown to support across a sequence of studies, including directional hysteresis, history-dependent perceptual reorganization, and body-grounded conative orientation, treating these as unified aspects of a single portable module.
There will then be a live demonstration attaching the perspective layer to an active inference agent, such as a hierarchical Bayesian / discrete state-space model, and running it in parallel with its unaugmented counterpart in the same environment, so participants can see exactly what the layer adds and where it plugs in.
The session closes with a structured discussion in which participants are invited to identify candidate insertion points for a perspective layer in their own active inference agents, whether built in PyMDP, RxInfer, or custom frameworks. The aim is to leave participants able to reason about whether and how a subjective perspective could be added.
presentations.title: A Modular Perspective Layer for Active Inference Agents
Active Inference and Free Energy Principle in 2026

presentations.abstract: Cognitive scientists have applied advances in our formal understanding of causation in philosophy and computer science, particularly within the Causal Bayes Net formalism, to understand human causal learning. This formalism is also closely related to ideas in active inference. In parallel, reinforcement learning researchers have developed the idea of an intrinsic reward signal called “empowerment”. An agent is rewarded for maximizing the mutual information between its actions and their outcomes, regardless of the external reward value of those outcomes. “Empowerment” may be an important bridge between classical Bayesian causal learning and reinforcement learning and may help to characterize causal learning in humans and enable it in machines
presentations.title: Active Inference, Bayesian Causal Learning and Empowerment in RL.

presentations.abstract:
How do we keep a coherent sense of self across time — and can that process be measured in real time, on consumer hardware, before it breaks down?
Root Frequency Theory (RFT) proposes that experiential continuity is not a default state but an ongoing biological achievement requiring coordination across five nested regulatory layers: environmental constraints (C0), autopoietic regulation (C1), predictive neural integration (C2), narrative self-organization (C3), and the continuity of lived experience (C4). Fragmentation is defined as a self-reinforcing cascade of cross-scale misalignment. The cascade is bidirectional: structured self-knowledge introduced at C3 — operationalized as epistemic alignment (Kₑ) — is hypothesized to initiate upward regulatory stabilization.
To test this, I developed the M-RFT metric: M = (Φ · Kₑ) / F, where Φ indexes autonomic flexibility via HRV, Kₑ composites interoceptive accuracy and narrative coherence, and F captures regulatory burden. I then built Root Extension — an iOS application using iPhone and Apple Watch — to administer this protocol ecologically and deliver personalized epistemic scaffolding upon session completion.
The N=1 longitudinal study ran 321 sessions across 23 active days (April 16–May 14, 2026), with the researcher as the sole subject. Key findings: mean M = 3.79 (Mdn = 2.14), intra-session regulatory recovery — FRAGMENTED to RESILIENT within the same calendar day — observed on 34.8% of active days.
This presentation introduces the theoretical architecture, the metric, the app protocol, and the preliminary data — and invites the active inference community into the next phase: a formal N=20–40 validation trial planned for 2027.
presentations.title: Root Frequency Theory: An Integrative Framework for the Continuity of Lived Experience

presentations.abstract: A live review of the Active Inference Institute’s 2026 Textbook Group on Sanjeev Namjoshi’s Fundamentals of Active Inference (2026). Since April 2026 the group has worked through the book chapter by chapter in open online meetings, with recorded sessions, shared meeting notes, a public question page, and an open-source companion repository of equations, methods, visualizations and animations. Facilitators Fraser Paterson, Andrew Pashea and Daniel Friedman look back on the chapters covered so far, the questions and stumbling blocks that came up along the way, and the resources the group has built, and discuss what it takes to learn Active Inference in 2026. Textbook Group participants and Symposium attendees are welcome to join the conversation live or through the livestream chat. The group continues with Chapter 13 after the Symposium and is open to new participants.

presentations.title: Learning Active Inference in 2026: Textbook Group Review

presentations.abstract: People naturally express their beliefs about a topic, situation, or problem in the form of narrative. CogNarr is a soon-to-be-released, open-source, interactive tool that lets a writer transform narrative into an explicit, formal semantic graph, which they can inspect and correct until it faithfully reflects their belief model. A CogNarr story graph captures a narrative's argument structure, its timing, and the modality of its claims, including predictions and conditionals, together with the uncertainty attached to each. In general it expresses the verifiable meaning of what a person wishes to say, while reducing the ambiguity of natural language. As such, it could be of use in modeling the beliefs that active-inference processes operate over, and as a framework within which active-inference methods could be employed to infer semantic meaning from text. Because it makes a person's beliefs explicit, transparent, and shareable, CogNarr has potential wherever consequential beliefs are expressed as narrative, from medicine and governance to public polling and accident reporting. As well, CogNarr story graphs support accurate agent-agent communication. The collective-cognition aim behind the project is alignment of shared belief models during decision-making processes in the large-group setting. The talk will be a preview of features and capabilities, with some discussion of potential applications.

presentations.title: CogNarr Story Graph: A Formal Semantics for Narrative as a Belief Model

presentations.abstract:
Active inference frames biological and cognitive agency as the imperatives of self-evidencing—maintaining systemic integrity by minimising variational free energy within an open, stochastic environment. Under this formalism, agents, from single cells to complex organisms, persist by regulating their internal states against entropic dissipation, enacting a Markov blanket that partitions self from world. This imperative entails sophisticated inference, balancing epistemic drives against pragmatic preferences, thereby constituting adaptive agency.
This talk extends this foundational picture of selfhood to the domain of political communities and global justice theory, demonstrating that the same dynamical constraints that govern individual persistence scale hierarchically to structure collective organisation and inter-state conduct. Drawing on the Free Energy Principle, political communities are modelled as open, self-organising systems embedded within a nested hierarchy of interacting Markov blankets. Their stability is not intrinsic but relational, contingent upon continuous exchange of information, resources, and institutional constraints with their environment.
Within this multiscale architecture, global justice emerges as an active regulatory imperative: a homeostatic constraint that maintains a nonequilibrium steady state across coupled societies. We formalise this through the expected free energy decomposition, where just policies balance risk—adherence to shared normative constraints such as human rights and non-aggression—against ambiguity—the active resolution of uncertainty arising from structural interdependence.
The normative implications are acute. We identify a pervasive pathology of self-organisation, wherein dominant or insular political regimes mis-specify themselves as closed systems. By suppressing external coupling and attenuating sensory evidence, they optimise local coherence at the expense of systemic stability. Drawing parallels to oncogenic cellular proliferation and psychotic cognitive inference, we argue that such closure systematically underestimates global risk and propagates destabilising volatility. Ultimately, we contend that justice is not a static distributive outcome nor a single-level contractual procedure, but the dynamic property of a multiscale system that successfully synchronises its trajectories under persistent uncertainty. This offers a unified, first-principles framework for linking the philosophy of agency to the normative demands of a deeply interconnected global order.

presentations.title: From Self-Evidencing to Global Governance: Active Inference and the Dynamics of Justice
“Evolution, Emergence, Prediction.”

presentations.abstract:
Political disagreement often reflects competing worldviews: different beliefs about how the world works and what will happen under alternative policies. Yet political debate proceeds linearly, through proposals, responses, and counterresponses. The underlying reasoning and evidence remain fragmented, assumptions can escape scrutiny, and criticism loses its target as debate moves on. Consequently, incompatible worldviews can persist without their disagreements being resolved.
This talk proposes a new politics, motivated by Active Inference, which provides the mathematical object around which political debate can be organized: the policy map. This map expresses a worldview through predicted outcomes under alternative policies. Making it the persistent object of debate allows criticism to retain a stable address rather than disappear in the rhetoric of successive exchanges.
The mathematics of the policy map distinguishes three types of criticism: belief criticism, challenging beliefs about current states or the consequences of policies; outcome incompleteness, identifying omitted consequences; and policy incompleteness, identifying missing alternatives. These provide the horizontal sorting of political debate.
Vertical sorting organizes the reasoning beneath each prediction, allowing criticism to reach its underlying assumptions and evidence. Unresolved objections remain visible until answered or incorporated through revision, potentially changing the predicted outcomes and preferred policies.
In this way, Active Inference offers a normative application that goes beyond describing politics as if political actors performed Bayesian inference. It motivates transforming the very structure of political debate, replacing rhetorical exchanges with cumulative criticism and incentivizing a shared search for the worldview that best fits the available evidence.
The ultimate aim is a politics in which criticism can actually bite, transforming not only political debates, but the world shaped by its decisions. For the only path forward is critique without exception.

presentations.title: A New Politics: From Linear to Sorted Politics Through the Policy Map

presentations.abstract:
Consciousness: The Channel Framework and its Application to INTREPID
The Channel Framework treats theories of consciousness as relating physical and experiential events, with the minimal relation being predictive. The Channel Framework embeds this psychophysical relation within the full experimental prediction architecture, connecting physical processes, conscious content, introspective access, and observable outcomes. Expressed through probabilistic channels, these architectures can be interpreted as generative models of experimental predictions, providing a common language in which different theories can be explicated and compared.
I apply the framework to INTREPID’s adversarial comparison of Integrated Information Theory and predictive-processing theories of consciousness, including Neurorepresentationalism and the Active Inference theory of consciousness (AI-C). The framework asks whether their prediction architectures can be faithfully aligned, which theoretical differences actually generate their contrasting experimental predictions, and whether these differences carry the particular claims the experiments aim to test.
Building on this analysis, the Channel Standard develops criteria for attributing evidence from competing theory predictions to specific theoretical claims. The broader aim is to move beyond theory-level comparison toward methodological concensus.

presentations.title: Explicating and Comparing Prediction Architectures of Theories of Consciousness and its Application to INTREPID

presentations.abstract: In this talk, I will review recent studies and results using active inference and related modeling approaches to study mechanisms of normative cognitive-affective processes and associated neural responses, and how these appear to be affected in different psychiatric conditions. I will also discuss contexts in which active inference appears to offer potentially unique resources for modeling these processes. Conversely, I will discuss contexts in which active inference may overlap with simpler modeling approaches and related issues centered around the level of mechanistic description one is interested in studying.
presentations.title: Recent advances in empirical applications of active inference in computational psychiatry

presentations.abstract: The claim that climate homeorhesis—non-equilibrium steady-state dynamics that underlie Earth’s long-term habitability—depends on an integrated biosphere–climate system capable of acting on its own is central to debates surrounding the Gaia hypothesis. This paper presents a proof of concept suggesting a minimal form of planetary agency based on a simple biosphere–climate system model operating through active inference. This means that the internal states of the system (biosphere) will appear to infer shifts in net incoming solar radiation (external states) through its boundary states, i.e. by integrating past and current surface temperatures (sensory states) and actively changing greenhouse forcing (active states) to maintain climate trajectories within geophysiological bounds. When surface temperature is altered by solar fluctuation changes, the system adjusts greenhouse and albedo parameters to restore expected climate trajectories, analogous to correcting sensory prediction errors in biological systems. Perturbing active states (e.g., imposed changes in albedo) does not reduce inference precision. Inference robustness decreases when the system’s degrees of freedom increase. Active inference falls, and thus climate homeorhesis fails when there is no biosphere activity (lifeless planet) or when it is decoupled from the climate system. Predictive behaviour operates within the range of solar constants consistent with life’s presence on Earth (~ 4 Ga to ~ 1.5 Ga expected in the future); outside this range, inference fails, undermining a putative form of planetary agency.
presentations.title: An elementary form of agency at planetary-scale

presentations.abstract:
Understanding biological intelligence requires identifying the variational invariant structures underlying neuronal dynamics. Experimental data provide access to the evolution of neural activity and synaptic weights. These dynamics can be expressed in different coordinates while preserving a common dynamical organisation. In Bayesian coordinates, they can be read as belief updating under an implicit generative model; in computational coordinates, as action generation, including behaviour, decision-making, and algorithmic computation. Triple equivalence formalises transformations among these descriptions and identifies their shared variational structure. The empirical question is which implicit generative model is instantiated by a given neuronal system.
Here, reverse engineering was applied to neural and behavioural data from zebrafish learning a visually guided go/no-go decision-making task. From initial neural activity, the method identified individual-specific implicit generative models and instantiated them as synthetic agents that minimise variational free energy. These agents generated trial-by-trial predictions of subsequent synaptic plasticity, neural activity, and behavioural performance. The predictions captured individual learning trajectories and generalised to previously unseen task conditions. Their agreement with unseen empirical data provides a quantitative test of the predictive validity of the free-energy principle in behaving animals. More broadly, this framework shows how present neuronal states can be used to forecast future learning and self-organisation in individual biological systems.
presentations.title: Reverse engineering generative models from zebrafish decision-making

presentations.abstract: If pymdp was an engine, Knowthyself is an attempt to give it a chassis and wheels. It’s beginner- and expert-friendly, fostering education, research and development, and maybe the idea of a “hub of digital twins” for currently existing literature. It comes in progressive levels of “difficulty” which unlock various tools and functionalities. You become a particular chemist, authoring all sort of “herds of strange things”.
